lines.note: Hiyori is weather or favourable conditions, glossed by tenki. Conjunção de tempo refers to a conjunction of weather circumstances, not a grammatical conjunction; the final Fi continues on the next line.
With the preceding Fi, hiyori ga yoi / warui means that the weather is good or bad. The contrast is explicit in bom / ruim; the short printed alternative marker l is not Japanese.
The weather is suitable or unsuitable for sailing. Nauegar is navegar in modern spelling; pera and the historical u/v usage remain unmodernized.
Hiyu, explained by tatoye, is a comparison or simile: 比喩 and たとえ. The Portuguese comparação confirms that this is not the plant named in the next entry.
A separate hiyu means an edible leafy plant, matched with Portuguese bredos (amaranth greens). The identical Japanese spelling does not mean the two entries should be merged.
Hiyuna adds na, a vegetable/greens element, to the preceding plant name. The scan reads Idem, referring to bredos; OCR's Ident was not a different botanical description.
Hiza is the knee. Hiza wo kaganuru means to bend the knees; the historical verb form should not be replaced with modern kagameru. Do continues as dobrar below.

runs.text: brar os joelhos, ou abaixarſe hum pouco.

lines.note: The Portuguese explains bending the knees or lowering oneself a little. Hum is the historical form of um; the line does not prescribe a particular seated posture yet.
Hiza wo tatsuru introduces a kneeling posture. The following lines are needed to understand what the dictionary calls the Japanese manner, rather than substituting a modern posture label.

runs.text: modo de Iapão que he estribãdo nos joelhos, &

lines.note: The posture supports the body on the knees, according to the dictionary's description. Estribãdo represents estribando; its nasal abbreviation and printed s form are retained.

runs.text: nas pontas dos pès deſcanſando as partes poſte-

lines.note: Support on the tips of the feet is also mentioned, with the posterior parts resting farther back. The adjective poste-riores continues into the next line; no missing Japanese phrase is implied.
Calcanhares are heels, completing the posture description. The next Japanese example begins hiza wo wo-ru, bend the knees; vo represents o, while uo marks the object particle.

The continuation completes woru, and kussuru is offered as an alternative, both translated as bending the knees. The two long s characters in cuſſuru belong to Japanese roman type, not the italic ß convention.
Hiza wo kumu means sitting with crossed legs. Aßentarſe is the Portuguese reflexive sit down, and cru continues as cruzadas; the unprinted line-end hyphen is not supplied.
Hizagumi wo suru gives a noun-plus-suru expression for the same crossed-leg posture. Idem points back to the preceding explanation, not to the earlier kneeling description.
Takahiza wo tatsuru introduces another kneeling posture. The visible paragraph sign and the faint r in Pòrſe were recovered; the next line specifies the European manner.
Europa, not Eucopa, is legible and contrasts with Iapão above. Hizamazzuku is another expression for kneeling; the printed zz belongs to the historical dz series.
Idem closes the preceding kneeling example. Hiza wo noburu then means stretching the knees or legs; noburu is a historical form and should not be modernized to nobasu in the transcription.
The phrase hiza wo nawosu changes the subject to adjusting one's posture. Portuguese Pòrſe a sua vontade, continued below, means making oneself comfortable rather than medical treatment of the knee.
Hiza wo nawosaxerarei is a polite invitation to relax one's knees/posture. The historical honorific ending is supported by the following courteous Portuguese imperative; Vt is italic.

runs.text: Estai a voßa vontade deſcanſando os joelhos.

lines.note: Estai a voßa vontade tells the addressee to be at ease, resting the knees. This confirms the pragmatic, polite sense of the preceding Japanese example.
Hizabushi names the joints or round structures of the knees. Nòs here means knots/joints, not the first-person pronoun nós; rodelas provides a second anatomical description.
Hizagashira is the kneecap, literally the head of the knee. The Portuguese again uses rodelas dos joelhos, associating it with the preceding anatomical entry.
Hizaguchi is explained as hiza no kuchi, literally the knee's opening/mouth. Idem equates its referent with the kneecap terms above without requiring us to normalize the Japanese compound.
Hizamazzuki gives the conjugational series of kneel. The abbreviated u and uita are dictionary endings, not independent words; the full verb is the same as Fizamazzuqu above.
Hizamoto means beside or at someone's knees. Iunto dos joelhos is a spatial explanation and leads naturally into the figurative court-attendant expression below.

runs.text: O que ſempre eſtà a ilhar-

lines.note: Hizamoto sarazu is literally not leaving the vicinity of the knees. The definition describes someone always at a lord's side; ilhar-ga is split across lines.
The attendant is described as a privado, an intimate or favourite of a lord. This completes the figurative sense rather than adding a new headword.
Hiza no sara, the knee's plate, names the kneecap. The scan's sara initial is long ſ; the Portuguese singular rodela do joelho agrees with this anatomical sense.
Hizashi here concerns fixing a day, not sunlight. O determinar o dia makes that homophony clear; hizashi wo continues into the next line's suru.
Hizashi wo suru means to determine a particular day. The Portuguese dia certo confirms appointment/date-setting rather than an action involving knees.
Hizori, with its printed conjugation series, is warping such as a board's. Empenarſe supports the intransitive sense; the unusual-looking spelling is not grounds for replacing the headword.
Hizzumakashi is a causative/transitive form, to make something crooked. Its aita ending illustrates historical s-verb i-onbin; it should not be regularized to an ashita ending.

runs.text: Vnhas de caualo, & de outros ani-

lines.note: Hizzume is the hoof, described as the nails of a horse and other animals. This literal Portuguese wording is broader than the modern English distinction between nail and hoof.
Hizzume no wareta kedamono is an animal with a divided hoof. Wareta modifies the hoof, not a broken animal; the split Portuguese animais belongs to the preceding definition.
Animal de vnha fendida confirms a cloven/divided hoof. The singular vnha is the historical u-initial spelling, not a Japanese word needing a reading hint.
Hizzumi is the intransitive counterpart, to become or be crooked. Entortarſe / estar torto distinguish process and state, and match the Japanese verb rather than the preceding hoof noun.

runs.text: Dia da data que ſe eſcreue na carta,

lines.note: Hizzuke is the written date on a letter. Dia da data clarifies that this is dating a document, not the act of deciding a day described under Fizaxi.
Other written documents are included. Hizzuke wo su-ru continues below, a normal noun-plus-suru construction; its line-end hyphen is visible.

runs.text: Eſcreuer o dia do mes em carta, &c.

lines.note: The example means to write the day of the month on a letter. Historical eſcreuer and mes are retained; the final &c. is part of the explanation.

The example asks what date the document bears. Iccano is retained as the scan's uncertain-looking spelling rather than silently changed to an expected interrogative such as itcuno; the visible paragraph mark was restored.

runs.text: data, ou quando foi eſcrita a carta? &c.

lines.note: The Portuguese restates the question as when the letter was written. The ending is carta? in the scan, not the OCR string cariae; the question closes before &c.
The large initial is F, giving fǒ (方), a side or direction, explained by kata. The example begins fǒ shisun, four sun square; the decorated letter spans two physical rows and is not an E.

runs.text: Colũna que tem de cada face

lines.note: Shisun no hashira completes a description of a square pillar. The first letter of faxira is f, not t: hashira and Portuguese colũna independently fit the visible word. Each face has the stated width.

Largura is width, not laegura. Shisun bǒ no hashira gives the same square-pillar expression with reversed order; b before ǒ is severely abraded, but its residual bowl/stem area and the corresponding fǒ shisun example support this provisional reading. The apparent comma in the OCR is not treated as Japanese punctuation.
Ra completes faxi-ra, hashira, and Idem refers to the same pillar. It is a body continuation above the bottom rule, not a catchword or a standalone word ta.

runs.text: Eſpiga de trigo, ou de outro legume, ou erua.

lines.note: Fo is the ear or spike of a plant, 穂, here illustrated by wheat and other plants. Legume has the dictionary's broad historical plant/seed usage; this is not the sailing sense introduced later.

Fǒ is a rule or established custom. Sadamatta fǒ gia means that it is a settled rule; the word after sadamatta starts with f, not r. The caron spelling is retained rather than harmonized with the next headword's circumflex.

runs.text: He lei posta, ou cuſtume ordinario. ¶

lines.note: Lei poſta means an established law, paired with ordinary custom. The abraded ſt sequence explains OCR's poila; fǒ wo continues into the next line's verb.
Fǒ wo wokasu is to violate a rule. Portuguese quebrar a lei ou cuſtume confirms the sense, and the missing long ſ in cuſtume was restored from the scan.
Fô is glossed nori, law or doctrine. Yaburu and somuku are alternatives for breaking or disobeying it; the faint Portuguese word is Lei, not Lti.
Qu completes somuku. Fô wo hiromuru then means to spread the law or teaching, with the historical hiromuru form preserved rather than modern hiromeru.
Dilatar a lei explains spreading the teaching, while fô wo toku is expounding it. The final Portuguese is Pregar a lei., preach the doctrine, with a visible period rather than the OCR hyphen.
Fô here is a method or prescription, specified as kusuri no fô. Regimento introduces a regimen or set of instructions; the small explanatory i has a visible comma.
Receita de mezinhas completes the medicinal-prescription sense. These are historical lexicographic meanings, not an endorsement of a medical regimen.
A different fô means the cheek. Maçaã do roſto is the Portuguese apple-of-the-face expression; the first abraded vowel after ç is a, not u. Fô wo utsu introduces striking the cheek.
Dar bofetada no rosto means to slap the face. Bofetada is printed as one word; the OCR's internal space was not a meaningful word boundary.
Fo now means a sail, 帆. Fo wo aguru, kakuru and hiku are alternatives for setting or hoisting it; the absence of a long-vowel accent distinguishes it from nearby fô entries.
Hiku completes the hoisting alternatives. Fo wo worosu means to lower the sail: the scan has Fouo, without the extra i supplied by OCR, and the Portuguese contrast supports this reading.
Saguru is the alternate lowering verb. Amainar a vela is the corresponding Portuguese sailing expression, not a reference to reducing the earlier law or doctrine.
Fôate is a face/cheek guard, described as a viseira. The headword's visible mark is a circumflex like that in Fôateuo, not a caron; the example means putting on the guard.
The guard is placed on the face. Rosto remains in its printed short-s form; semantic interpretation does not justify normalizing that allograph.

runs.text: Doença que faz inchar o roſto. No

lines.note: Fôbare names a condition of swollen cheeks/face. The dictionary supplies a regional alternative next; the description is historical and does not establish a modern clinical diagnosis.

In the Cami the form is fôfare, an unvoiced counterpart to fôbare. Both the alternative and the following Fôbareuo show circumflex marks in the scan; Cami itself is italic within the Portuguese explanation.

runs.text: Estar com o roſto inchado desta doença.

lines.note: Ya-mu completes the phrase for suffering from this swelling. Portuguese estar com o rosto inchado explicitly links it to the preceding condition rather than a general sorrow sense of yamu.
Fǒbai is a companion or fellow, 傍輩. Its caron is visible and should not be assimilated to the adjacent cheek compounds with circumflexes.
Fobashira, literally sail-pillar, is a mast. The example begins fo-bashira wo tatsuru, raising it; the historical Portuguese masto is retained rather than changed to mastro.
Woshitatsuru is an alternative for erecting the mast. Aleuantar o masto supplies a direct semantic check on both Japanese verbs.

runs.text: Ardil, ou modo de enſinar o Fotoque

lines.note: Fǒben is an expedient way of teaching, 方便. The Portuguese describes it polemically as an ardil; this is the compiler's framing, not a neutral definition of Buddhist doctrine. Fotoque is visibly upright inside the italic explanation.

runs.text: com doctrina apparente pera que o pouo ſe affei

lines.note: The explanation says the teaching is presented so that the people become attached to it. Affei-çoe is split without a printed hyphen; the final i is visible in the enlarged scan, replacing OCR's r.

runs.text: çoe, poſto que em ſecreto tenha, & enſine ou-

lines.note: The compiler contrasts the public teaching with what is supposedly held and taught in secret. This is part of the same polemical definition, not a statement independently verified by the transcription project.
Tra completes outra couſa, something else, and closes the fǒben definition. The line is short but real body text; it should not be merged geometrically with the following cosmetic entry.
Fôbeni is cheek rouge, with beni providing the colour/cosmetic element. The headword's e was misread as c by OCR; rebique is a historical Portuguese term for face colouring.
Sasu, tsukuru and nuru are listed for applying the rouge. Portuguese Pòr rebique confirms the cosmetic noun; its damaged b should not be transcribed as o.
Fôbera first names fish gills, then a region of the human face. Par continues into parte below, without adding an editorial line-end hyphen.

runs.text: te do roſto das meçaãs pera baixo. i,

lines.note: The second sense extends downward from the cheeks, with fôta-bura supplied as a Japanese equivalent. The printed maçaã-type historical spelling is not normalized to modern maçãs.
Bura completes fôtabura. The following B. is visibly roman, a usage label rather than part of the Japanese word or a new entry.
Fôbi means praise or reward, 褒美, explained by home itsukushimu. Louuor / premio supports this interpretation; the circumflex belongs to the source spelling, not to a modern kana normalization.
Fôbi suru means rewarding someone. The small circumflex above ô is visible in the scan, although omitted by OCR; al-gum continues across the line break.
The reward is for some service. Fôbi wo nasu supplies another Japanese construction, with the same visible circumflex and the object marker wo.

Gofôbi aru / nasaruru are honorific formulations about rewarding. The damaged f and visible circumflex distinguish Gofôbi from OCR's Gorǒbi; the following noble-person qualification independently fits go- and nasaruru.
Falando de peßoa nobre limits the preceding expressions to a noble person. The note concerns register rather than a separate meaning of the headword.

runs.text: Todas as partes, ou varias partes.

lines.note: Fǒbǒ means all or various directions/places, 方々. Both carons are clearly marked, unlike the preceding reward compound.
Fǒbǒ wo kakete ariku describes going around different places. The paragraph mark is visible at the left and was restored; ariku is retained as the historical verb form.
Diuerſas partes e lugares completes the travel explanation. Lugares, places, is readable in the scan and replaces the meaningless OCR luzars.
Fobo is hobo, approximately or for the most part, explained by woyoso. Adu. is italic, while the Japanese words and explanatory i remain roman.
Fobo moxi ireta means communicating something roughly or in general outline. The next Portuguese line makes the approximation explicit; moxi is the historical polite speaking form.

runs.text: pouco mais, ou menos lhe diſſe.

lines.note: Pouco mais ou menos lhe diſſe means that one told it more or less approximately. The word is mais, not mats; the source's two-long-s spelling in diſſe is retained.
Fǒbocu is a courteous term for a letter, 芳墨. Carta and falando com corteſia establish both the referent and register; Vt introduces its example.

Fǒbocu haiken seshime soro is a formal epistolary acknowledgement. The Portuguese translates it as receiving the addressee's letter; the written soro is retained without supplying unseen long-vowel marks.
Voßa mercè supplies the polite addressee in the Portuguese acknowledgement. This completes the preceding sentence, not a new heading or label.

Fôbon is a square tray, explained as yofô no bon. The definition and Japanese paraphrase agree on four-sided shape; no attempt is made to regularize the printed vowel marks by modern lexical expectation.
Fôbone is the cheekbone. Oßos das maçaãs do rosto gives the literal bones-of-the-cheeks explanation; the Fôbu- below is the separate catchword for the next page.
